html:
Camera translating sideways
Five copies of the same camera, shifted along X. Red arrows = translation T, always parallel to the image plane.
View
Move the slider or press play to release a movable blue camera along the strip.
Guided demo
Hover or click any frustum, arrow or scene point for an explanation. Drag to orbit out of the printed front view — the red arrows stay inside the image plane, so the forward velocity component is exactly zero. “Reset View” returns to the figure pose.
⚠ Figure failed to load

elements: Five identical wireframe camera frusta in one horizontal row, evenly spaced, identical size and identical orientation (no scaling, no rotation between copies)
For each camera: a solid black dot (projection center / optical center) at the bottom of the glyph, nearest the viewer
For each camera: four straight edges rising from the projection-center dot to the four corners of the image-plane rectangle
For each camera: the wide image-plane rectangle drawn as a closed quadrilateral above and behind the dot

For each camera: a horizontal band line across the rectangle plus two lines crossing from the band's outer corners down to the rectangle's lower corners, giving the 'pyramid seen from behind and slightly below' read
Six thick horizontal red arrows along the baseline of the strip: one leading the leftmost camera, one in each of the four gaps, one trailing off the right edge, all arrowheads pointing right
Implied straight translation axis through all five projection centers, parallel to the image planes (shown only in the annotated view)
Optical axis of each camera pointing away from the viewer, perpendicular to the translation axis (shown only in the annotated view)
Two scene points at different depths (near point, far point) used in the optical-flow view
Projection rays from the two scene points to the active camera's center (flow view only)
Projected image dots of the near and far points on the active camera's image plane (flow view only)
Red 2-D flow vectors on the image plane whose length scales as f*Tx/Z (flow view only)
Faded ghost outlines of the inactive camera poses marking the straight lateral path (flow view only)

interactions.teaches: The plain strip is the source figure; adding axes proves the motion vector lies in the image plane and is perpendicular to every optical axis; switching to the image view shows that nearer points sweep across faster than far ones.
interactions.label: View

interactions.teaches: Lateral displacement changes only the camera's X position — orientation and depth are untouched, and the image shift it produces is dx = -f*Tx/Z.
interactions.label: Lateral displacement Tx (units)

interactions.teaches: Continuous sideways travel parallel to the image plane makes the whole scene stream across the frame — the side-window-of-a-moving-car percept — with zero forward velocity component.
interactions.label: Play lateral translation

interactions.teaches: Rotating away from the flat front-on elevation reveals the frusta really point away from the viewer, so the red arrows run perpendicular to the line of sight rather than along it.
interactions.type_note: returns to the front-on default on reset

demo_steps.title: The source strip
demo_steps.narration: Five identical camera frusta stand in a row, each aiming away from you, separated by bold red arrows all pointing right. Nothing about the camera changes except where it sits.

demo_steps.title: Slide it sideways
demo_steps.narration: Drag the displacement slider: one camera travels the whole row while its optical axis stays locked. Every intermediate pose coincides with one of the five drawn glyphs.

demo_steps.title: Motion is perpendicular to the line of sight
demo_steps.narration: Turn on the annotations: the translation axis (red) runs left-right in the image plane while the optical axis (dashed) points away from you. Their dot product is zero, so the forward velocity component is exactly zero.

demo_steps.title: What the image sees
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the projected view. As the camera slides right, both scene points slide left across the image — the classic side-window sweep.

demo_steps.title: Near beats far: parallax
demo_steps.narration: At full displacement the near point's flow vector is three times longer than the far point's, for the same camera travel. Image shift scales as translation divided by depth.

plan.geometry_notes: DEFAULT VIEW IS A FLAT FRONT-ON ORTHOGRAPHIC ELEVATION: orthographic camera at (0, 0, +18) looking down -Z, up = +Y, no tilt, no azimuth — the five glyphs must project exactly as in the source (wide rectangle up top, black dot below it, four converging edges). Orbit is the only thing that leaves this pose. Fit the ortho frustum to X = -8.2 .. +8.2 (strip fills the full canvas width); Y = -2.6 .. +2.0. CAMERA GLYPH (built once, instanced 5x with zero variation): image-plane rectangle 1.75 wide (X, screen-right) x 0.95 tall (Y, screen-up), lying in the plane Z = -0.9, centered at local (0, +0.50, -0.90); projection-center dot = black sphere radius 0.11 at local (0, -0.62, +0.90), i.e. below and toward the viewer. Four straight black edges connect the dot to the four rectangle corners. A horizontal band line crosses the rectangle at local Y = +0.30 spanning its full width, and two lines run from that band's left and right ends down to the rectangle's lower-left and lower-right corners, producing the 'seen from behind and slightly below' pyramid read. Optical axis = local -Z (away from the viewer); it is exactly perpendicular to the translation axis (+X). CAMERA CENTERS at X = -6, -3, 0, +3, +6, all Y = 0, Z = 0, identical orientation, perfectly collinear. RED ARROWS: 6 flat arrows, pure red #FF0000, drawn coplanar with the apex dots at Z = +0.90 and Y = -1.70; shaft 2.05 long x 0.26 thick, arrowhead 0.70 long x 0.72 wide, total length 2.75; centers at X = -7.5, -4.5, -1.5, +1.5, +4.5, +7.5 so one leads the row, four sit in the gaps, one trails off the right edge. All wireframe lines pure black #000000 at ~2.5 px constant width; background pure white #FFFFFF. NO tick labels, no axis text, no dashed guides in the default 'Camera strip' view — it must be graphically identical to the source. ANNOTATED PATH view adds: a thin red translation axis line along Y = 0, Z = 0 from X = -7.5 to +7.5, short dashed grey optical-axis stubs of length 1.4 from each dot along -Z, and a single small right-angle marker at the origin; keep text to at most two short labels ('Tx' and 'optical axis'). FLOW VIEW: near point at world (0.9, 0.6, -4.0), far point at (-0.7, 0.9, -12.0); focal length f = 1.4; image shift dx = -f*Tx/Z, so Z = 4 shifts 3x more than Z = 12. Flow arrows drawn in #FF0000 on the active camera's image plane; inactive frusta fade to 18% opacity grey ghosts.
plan.notes: Use THREE.OrthographicCamera for the default pose (not a perspective camera) so the glyphs read as a flat technical elevation; OrbitControls attached but starting exactly at azimuth 0 / elevation 0 relative to -Z, with a 'reset view' snap back to front-on. Build one camera glyph as a reusable Group of Line2/LineSegments (LineMaterial, linewidth ~2.5, resolution-aware) plus a small black sphere, then clone it five times along X — never rebuild or rescale per copy. Red arrows: flat ExtrudeGeometry/ShapeGeometry arrow outlines in the XY plane with MeshBasicMaterial 0xFF0000 (unlit) so they stay bold and uniform at any zoom; they must sit in front of the frusta lines (renderOrder higher, depthTest off) as in the source. In 'Projected optical flow' keep the active frustum solid, render its image plane as a 15% white quad, and draw projected dots + red flow arrows on it; optionally an inset face-on 2-D panel in a screen-space corner. The animation loops slideCamera from -6 to +6 over ~6 s linearly and draws a faint dashed trail along the camera centers; pausing it hands control back to the slider.

authoredPrompt: This figure is a horizontal strip in which the same wireframe camera appears five times, evenly spaced across a white field and interleaved with thick red arrows. Each camera is a viewing frustum seen from behind and slightly below: a solid black dot at the bottom marks the projection center, four straight edges rise from it to the corners of a wide rectangle standing for the image plane, and lines cross that rectangle to its lower corners, so the pyramid reads as pointing up and away from the viewer. The five copies match exactly in size and orientation. Red arrows run horizontally along the base of the strip, one before the leftmost camera, one in each of the four gaps, and one trailing off the right edge, every arrowhead pointing right. Because the frusta aim away from the viewer while the arrows travel across the picture, the motion is perpendicular to the line of sight rather than along it. The sequence illustrates sideways camera motion parallel to the image plane, as when a scene slides past the side window of a moving car, in which the forward velocity component is zero.
authoredInteractions:
- Animation for sliding the camera sideways parallel to the image plane; the frustum translates across the strip while projected scene points shift laterally, showing motion with zero forward component.
- Slider for lateral displacement; the active camera moves from left to right and image-plane vectors lengthen with the displacement, making the relation between side motion and apparent image shift explicit.
- Toggle between the 3-D path and projected optical flow for near versus far points; the flow view shows larger shifts for nearer points, connecting lateral translation to depth-dependent parallax.
authoredContext:
Consider a camera translating laterally, as shown in
the figure. This will happen if you are looking
through a side window of a car at the scene passing by. In this case,
the forward velocity is zero, $V_Z=0$.

Lateral camera motion parallel to the camera plane.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Strip is wide and short: total span X = -7 to +7, Y = -2 to +1.5. CAMERA GLYPH (one unit, repeated 5x identically, no scaling): image-plane rectangle 1.7 (X, screen-right) x 0.95 (Y, screen-up), centered at local (0, 0.55, 0); projection-center dot a black sphere of radius 0.10 at local (0, -0.55, +0.55) i.e. below and toward the viewer. Four straight edges join the dot to the four rectangle corners. Two additional lines run from the rectangle's upper-left and upper-right corners down to its lower-left/lower-right corners, and a second slightly smaller rectangle edge pair near the bottom of the face gives the 'viewed from behind and below' read. Optical axis points +Z away from viewer and slightly up (-Z into screen for the viewing direction); it is PERPENDICULAR to the translation axis. Camera centers at X = -6, -3, 0, +3, +6, all at Y = 0, Z = 0 — perfectly collinear, identical orientation. RED ARROWS: 6 of them, #FF0000, shaft thickness ~0.16, total length ~1.9 each, arrowhead ~0.45 long and ~0.45 wide, all lying at Y = -1.35, Z = +0.4, pointing +X; centered at X = -7.5, -4.5, -1.5, +1.5, +4.5, +7.5 so each sits in a gap (plus one leading, one trailing). All wireframe lines pure black #000000, line width ~2.5px, on white #FFFFFF background. FLOW VIEW: near point at world (0.8, 0.6, -4), far point at (-0.6, 0.9, -12). Projection with focal length f = 1.4 onto the active camera's image plane; image shift for pure lateral translation Tx is dx = -f*Tx/Z, so the near point (Z=4) shifts 3x more than the far point (Z=12). Flow arrows drawn in red on the image-plane rectangle, lengths proportional to |f*Tx/Z|.
interactionPlan.notes: Build one camera glyph as a reusable THREE.Group of LineSegments plus a small black sphere, and instance it five times along X — do not rebuild or vary it. Use LineBasicMaterial (or Line2/LineMaterial for consistent 2.5px width) in black. Red arrows: extruded flat shapes or Mesh boxes + cone-like triangular heads in the XY plane, MeshBasicMaterial 0xFF0000, unlit, so they read as flat graphic arrows. Camera: orthographic-feel axonometric pose, wide aspect framing (the figure is ~6:1), so fit the orthographic frustum to X span 14 and let heightFraction control vertical fill. In 'Projected optical flow' mode, fade the four inactive frusta to 18% opacity ghosts, keep the active frustum solid, and render the image-plane rectangle of the active camera as a semi-transparent white quad with the projected dots and red flow arrows drawn on it; optionally add a small inset 2-D panel showing the image plane face-on. Animation loops the slideCamera value from -6 to +6 over ~6s with linear easing and leaves a dashed trail line along the camera centers.

discrepancies: Source shows a strict front-on 2D silhouette of each camera glyph (rectangle with a horizontal band, two crossing diagonals, four edges converging to a dot below). The generated glyphs are viewed at a strong oblique azimuth (~109°) so the rectangles appear skewed/foreshortened and the crossing-diagonal pattern reads as a jumble — the iconic frustum silhouette is much less recognizable.

Red arrows in the source are thick, bold, uniform and lie exactly along the baseline at the same size; in the render they are thinner, tilted in the oblique view and vary in apparent length, weakening the strip motif.

The source figure is unlabelled; the generated version adds several annotations (x = -6 … x = 6, 'active camera', 'optical axis', 'translation T ∥ image plane') plus a highlighted blue camera, dashed translation axis and optical-axis cone — reasonable pedagogy but elements not present in the original.
Generated figure occupies only a small fraction of the canvas (scene is tiny in the left-of-panel area), whereas the source is a full-width strip; composition is much less impactful.

Camera glyph proportions differ: in the source the apex dot sits directly beneath the rectangle very close to its lower edge, and the inner band is a thin strip; in the render the apex is offset in depth (z = 0.55) producing a slanted pyramid rather than the flat frontal frustum.
evaluation.notes: Topology of the five-frustum strip with interleaved red arrows is correct and the interactions (slider, play, path/flow toggle, 4-step guided demo) are rich and conceptually apt, but the strongly oblique default camera and small on-screen scale make the iconic frontal frustum silhouette hard to recognize versus the source.
action_items: Set the default view much closer to front-on (azimuth ~180°, small elevation) so each glyph reads as the source's rectangle + band + crossing diagonals + apex dot, reserving oblique views for user orbiting.
Increase heightFraction / zoom so the five-camera strip fills the canvas width like the source's full-width band.
Thicken and lengthen the red arrows (and place them coplanar with the strip baseline) so they match the bold uniform arrows of the original.
Reduce annotation clutter in the default 'path' view (e.g. hide the x = … tick labels or shrink the optical-axis/translation-axis dashes) so the plain source-like composition dominates initially.
plan_action_items: Specify a front-on orthographic default projection for the base strip panel, since the source is a flat orthographic elevation of the camera glyphs.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interactions are sound, but the plan lacks a specified front-on orthographic default projection/scale for the strip, which drives the Camera-Wrong faithfulness failures and the critic's explicit plan action item.

discrepancies: Frustum glyph proportions differ: in the source the pinhole dot sits well below the rectangle with a clearly flared trapezoid (its side edges extend slightly outside the rectangle's width), while the generated glyph's apex sits almost on the rectangle's bottom edge, producing a much shallower, narrower cone under a proportionally larger box.

Spacing/scale: the generated red arrows nearly touch (and visually collide with) the frusta, whereas the source keeps clear white gaps between each arrow and the adjacent camera; the arrows are also thinner/shorter relative to the glyph than in the print.
Added red caption 'translation T ∥ image plane ( ⊥ optical axis )' below the strip has no counterpart in the source figure (harmless pedagogically, but an addition).
The inner horizontal band line of each glyph is faint/near the very bottom edge in the render, so the two-tier 'box + band' look of the printed glyph reads less clearly.

Overall strip is drawn dead front-on with no depth cue at all; the source line drawing already implies a 3D frustum viewed slightly obliquely (visible converging edges), so the printed glyph reads more three-dimensional than the render's default pose.
evaluation.notes: Composition, glyph count, arrow count and color scheme closely reproduce the printed strip and the interaction set (slider, play, mode toggle, annotation checkbox, 5-step guided demo, hover explanations) is rich and conceptually correct; main weaknesses are frustum proportions (apex too close to the image rectangle, no flare) and arrows crowding the glyphs, plus a slightly small default caption.
action_items: Move the pinhole apex further below the image rectangle and flare the frustum edges so the four edges pass outside the rectangle's bottom corners, matching the printed glyph silhouette.

elements: Five identical wireframe camera frusta in one horizontal row, evenly spaced, identical size and identical orientation (no scaling, no rotation between copies)
For each camera: a solid black dot (projection center / optical center) at the bottom of the glyph, nearest the viewer
For each camera: four straight edges rising from the projection-center dot to the four corners of the image-plane rectangle
For each camera: the wide image-plane rectangle drawn as a closed quadrilateral above and behind the dot

For each camera: a horizontal band line across the rectangle plus two lines crossing from the band's outer corners down to the rectangle's lower corners, giving the 'pyramid seen from behind and slightly below' read
Six thick horizontal red arrows along the baseline of the strip: one leading the leftmost camera, one in each of the four gaps, one trailing off the right edge, all arrowheads pointing right
Implied straight translation axis through all five projection centers, parallel to the image planes (shown only in the annotated view)
Optical axis of each camera pointing away from the viewer, perpendicular to the translation axis (shown only in the annotated view)
Two scene points at different depths (near point, far point) used in the optical-flow view
Projection rays from the two scene points to the active camera's center (flow view only)
Projected image dots of the near and far points on the active camera's image plane (flow view only)
Red 2-D flow vectors on the image plane whose length scales as f*Tx/Z (flow view only)
Faded ghost outlines of the inactive camera poses marking the straight lateral path (flow view only)

interactions.teaches: The plain strip is the source figure; adding axes proves the motion vector lies in the image plane and is perpendicular to every optical axis; switching to the image view shows that nearer points sweep across faster than far ones.
interactions.label: View

interactions.teaches: Lateral displacement changes only the camera's X position — orientation and depth are untouched, and the image shift it produces is dx = -f*Tx/Z.
interactions.label: Lateral displacement Tx (units)

interactions.teaches: Continuous sideways travel parallel to the image plane makes the whole scene stream across the frame — the side-window-of-a-moving-car percept — with zero forward velocity component.
interactions.label: Play lateral translation

interactions.teaches: Rotating away from the flat front-on elevation reveals the frusta really point away from the viewer, so the red arrows run perpendicular to the line of sight rather than along it.
interactions.type_note: returns to the front-on default on reset

demo_steps.title: The source strip
demo_steps.narration: Five identical camera frusta stand in a row, each aiming away from you, separated by bold red arrows all pointing right. Nothing about the camera changes except where it sits.

demo_steps.title: Slide it sideways
demo_steps.narration: Drag the displacement slider: one camera travels the whole row while its optical axis stays locked. Every intermediate pose coincides with one of the five drawn glyphs.

demo_steps.title: Motion is perpendicular to the line of sight
demo_steps.narration: Turn on the annotations: the translation axis (red) runs left-right in the image plane while the optical axis (dashed) points away from you. Their dot product is zero, so the forward velocity component is exactly zero.

demo_steps.title: What the image sees
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the projected view. As the camera slides right, both scene points slide left across the image — the classic side-window sweep.

demo_steps.title: Near beats far: parallax
demo_steps.narration: At full displacement the near point's flow vector is three times longer than the far point's, for the same camera travel. Image shift scales as translation divided by depth.

plan.geometry_notes: DEFAULT VIEW IS A FLAT FRONT-ON ORTHOGRAPHIC ELEVATION: orthographic camera at (0, 0, +18) looking down -Z, up = +Y, no tilt, no azimuth — the five glyphs must project exactly as in the source (wide rectangle up top, black dot below it, four converging edges). Orbit is the only thing that leaves this pose. Fit the ortho frustum to X = -8.2 .. +8.2 (strip fills the full canvas width); Y = -2.6 .. +2.0. CAMERA GLYPH (built once, instanced 5x with zero variation): image-plane rectangle 1.75 wide (X, screen-right) x 0.95 tall (Y, screen-up), lying in the plane Z = -0.9, centered at local (0, +0.50, -0.90); projection-center dot = black sphere radius 0.11 at local (0, -0.62, +0.90), i.e. below and toward the viewer. Four straight black edges connect the dot to the four rectangle corners. A horizontal band line crosses the rectangle at local Y = +0.30 spanning its full width, and two lines run from that band's left and right ends down to the rectangle's lower-left and lower-right corners, producing the 'seen from behind and slightly below' pyramid read. Optical axis = local -Z (away from the viewer); it is exactly perpendicular to the translation axis (+X). CAMERA CENTERS at X = -6, -3, 0, +3, +6, all Y = 0, Z = 0, identical orientation, perfectly collinear. RED ARROWS: 6 flat arrows, pure red #FF0000, drawn coplanar with the apex dots at Z = +0.90 and Y = -1.70; shaft 2.05 long x 0.26 thick, arrowhead 0.70 long x 0.72 wide, total length 2.75; centers at X = -7.5, -4.5, -1.5, +1.5, +4.5, +7.5 so one leads the row, four sit in the gaps, one trails off the right edge. All wireframe lines pure black #000000 at ~2.5 px constant width; background pure white #FFFFFF. NO tick labels, no axis text, no dashed guides in the default 'Camera strip' view — it must be graphically identical to the source. ANNOTATED PATH view adds: a thin red translation axis line along Y = 0, Z = 0 from X = -7.5 to +7.5, short dashed grey optical-axis stubs of length 1.4 from each dot along -Z, and a single small right-angle marker at the origin; keep text to at most two short labels ('Tx' and 'optical axis'). FLOW VIEW: near point at world (0.9, 0.6, -4.0), far point at (-0.7, 0.9, -12.0); focal length f = 1.4; image shift dx = -f*Tx/Z, so Z = 4 shifts 3x more than Z = 12. Flow arrows drawn in #FF0000 on the active camera's image plane; inactive frusta fade to 18% opacity grey ghosts.
plan.notes: Use THREE.OrthographicCamera for the default pose (not a perspective camera) so the glyphs read as a flat technical elevation; OrbitControls attached but starting exactly at azimuth 0 / elevation 0 relative to -Z, with a 'reset view' snap back to front-on. Build one camera glyph as a reusable Group of Line2/LineSegments (LineMaterial, linewidth ~2.5, resolution-aware) plus a small black sphere, then clone it five times along X — never rebuild or rescale per copy. Red arrows: flat ExtrudeGeometry/ShapeGeometry arrow outlines in the XY plane with MeshBasicMaterial 0xFF0000 (unlit) so they stay bold and uniform at any zoom; they must sit in front of the frusta lines (renderOrder higher, depthTest off) as in the source. In 'Projected optical flow' keep the active frustum solid, render its image plane as a 15% white quad, and draw projected dots + red flow arrows on it; optionally an inset face-on 2-D panel in a screen-space corner. The animation loops slideCamera from -6 to +6 over ~6 s linearly and draws a faint dashed trail along the camera centers; pausing it hands control back to the slider.

discrepancies: The camera frusta in the generated figure are drawn noticeably smaller relative to the arrow lengths than in the source, where the boxes are large and clearly dominate the strip; arrows appear proportionally long/thick.

Source glyphs show a distinct two-tier box (a horizontal band near the bottom) plus frustum lines flaring outside the bottom corners to a large pinhole dot; the generated glyph's pinhole dot is very small and the flare/band structure reads less clearly at the default scale.

Source figure has no text labels at all; the generated default view hides labels (annotations off) which matches, but the extra scene points, optical axis, blue active camera and flow view are additions beyond the source (acceptable as teaching extras, but they are hallucinated content relative to the source).

The frusta are effectively coplanar flat line drawings viewed front-on; there is essentially no 3D depth in the default figure (correct for the source, but the glyphs themselves are flat 2D wireframes rather than actual 3D frusta, so orbiting reveals no volumetric structure for the camera boxes).
evaluation.notes: Composition, arrow pattern, and glyph topology closely match the source and the interaction set (slider, play, view toggle, annotation checkbox, 5-step guided demo) is rich and conceptually correct; main weaknesses are undersized frusta relative to the arrows and flat, non-volumetric camera glyphs that show no real 3D structure when orbited.
